items.title: Jihad has greater and lesser meanings in classical Islam
items.claim: What is the greater/lesser jihad distinction?

options.text: Both refer only to armed warfare

A widely cited hadith distinguishes lesser jihad (armed struggle in defence of the community) from greater jihad (inner struggle against one's own ego); the hadith's authenticity is debated but the inner-struggle understanding is found in independent Sufi and mainstream piety traditions
Jihad refers only to economic struggle

items.reveal:
The Arabic root j-h-d means 'to strive, to exert effort'. The greater/lesser distinction is attributed to a hadith reported by al-Bayhaqi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi: 'We have returned from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the jihad against the self.'

Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) and some modern scholars question the hadith's chain of authentication. But the inner-struggle theme appears widely in Sufi writing and is not dependent on the hadith alone.

Classical Islamic law (fiqh) regulates armed jihad with conditions on declaration, conduct, and protection of non-combatants — distinct from later extremist appropriations of the term.
items.why: A word picked up by 21st-century media can carry meanings that don't match its theological tradition. 'Jihad' in classical Islam is far more various than its English-language press usage.

items.title: Judaism centres on covenant — a binding agreement with God
items.claim: What is the relationship between the Abrahamic and Mosaic covenants in Judaism?

options.text: The Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17, sealed by circumcision) promises land and descendants; the Mosaic covenant (Exodus 19-24, at Sinai) gives the Torah law — both remain binding on Jews
There is only one covenant — at Sinai
Covenants applied only to ancient Israelites, not modern Jews

items.reveal:
Brit milah (covenant of circumcision) is performed on Jewish boys on the eighth day after birth, marking the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 17:11-13). The Mosaic covenant at Sinai (around 1300 BCE in traditional dating) establishes the 613 mitzvot (commandments) of the Torah law.

The Noahide covenant (Genesis 9) — applying to all humanity — is also recognised. Rabbinic Judaism distinguishes seven Noahide laws binding on all people from the 613 mitzvot binding specifically on Jews.

Christianity reinterprets these covenants through 'new covenant' theology (Hebrews 8); Judaism rejects supersessionism — the older covenants are not abrogated.
items.why: Covenant is not a vague concept of relationship. In Judaism it is a specific structure with terms, obligations and consequences — and a major point of theological disagreement with Christianity.

items.title: Aristotelian virtue ethics aims at eudaimonia (flourishing)
items.claim: What is eudaimonia in Aristotle's ethics?

options.text: Flourishing or living well — the proper end of human life. The virtues (excellences of character) are stable dispositions developed through habituation that enable a person to function well as a human being

items.reveal:
Aristotle's 'Nicomachean Ethics' (Book I) argues that all human action aims at some good; there must be a highest good — eudaimonia.

The ergon (function) argument: humans, like everything, have a characteristic function — rational activity in accordance with virtue. The virtues are not lists of good behaviours but stable dispositions developed through habituation.

The doctrine of the mean: each virtue lies between two vices (courage between cowardice and recklessness; generosity between miserliness and profligacy).

Alasdair MacIntyre's 'After Virtue' (1981) revived virtue ethics by arguing modern moral discourse has lost the framework that gives moral vocabulary its meaning.
items.why: Virtue ethics is not 'be a good person'. It is a structured theory with specific terms — function, habituation, the mean, flourishing — linking character to the good life in a way that act-based theories do not.
